kurals.tamil:
ஒளிஒருவற்கு உள்ள வெறுக்கை இளிஒருவற்கு
அஃதிறந்து வாழ்தும் எனல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Olioruvarku ulla verukkai ilioruvarku
ahdhirandhu vaazhdhum enal.
kurals.meaning: A person's shining glory is an abundance of inner drive; a person's disgrace is the thought, 'I will get through life without it.'
kurals.elementary: Some kids say, 'I will try the hard puzzle!' and their faces light up. Others say, 'I'll just skip it and sit.' Valluvar says the first kind of heart is what makes a person shine, and the lazy 'I'll just skip it' is what makes a person small.
kurals.university: The chapter opens by defining greatness as an inner quality rather than a rank: oli (ஒளி, 'light, lustre, renown') is ulla verukkai (உள்ள வெறுக்கை), literally 'the wealth/abundance of the mind', which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses as ஊக்கமிகுதி ('excess of zeal') and Puliyur Kesikan, following the older commentarial line descending from Parimelazhagar, as the resolve 'I will do what others find hard to do'. Its opposite, ili (இளி, 'disgrace'), is not failure but the attitude ahdhirandhu vaazhdhum enal (அஃதிறந்து வாழ்தும் எனல்), 'saying we shall live having let it go'. Pope's 'The light of life is mental energy' follows the majority reading; Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh reads verukkai as வெறுமை ('emptiness of mind'), a contemplative minority interpretation not shared by the classical glosses. Placed in the Kudiyiyal after Maanam (Honour, ch. 97), the chapter moves from guarding one's dignity to the active, self-effacing greatness of the noble. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Pṛthā, do not yield to this degrading impotence. It does not become you. Give up such petty weakness of heart and arise, O chastiser of the enemy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells the despondent Arjuna that giving up in faintheartedness is beneath him and urges him to rise to his task.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it calls the loss of spirit a disgrace and summons a person back to energetic effort.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.3 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; strong match on spirit-versus-shameful-slackness, though the Gita's setting is a warrior's duty in battle.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher urges wholehearted effort in every task because life's chance to act is brief.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts prize the full-strength drive to act over a life coasting without it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; shares the praise of vigorous effort but lacks the Kural's explicit naming of slackness as disgrace.

islam.quote_or_event: “And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an teaches that a person's portion is tied to their own striving.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it locates a person's worth in their own effort rather than in what they happen to have.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a sound thematic link on striving, but the verse concerns moral accountability rather than greatness or disgrace.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Judah ben Tema said: Be strong as a leopard, and swift as an eagle, and fleet as a gazelle, and brave as a lion, to do the will of your Father who is in heaven.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah demands boldness, speed and courage in carrying out what is right.
judaism.tie_back: It pictures exactly the abundance of inner energy that the Kural calls a person's light.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 5:20 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; vivid match for zeal, though it aims that zeal at divine service rather than at personal greatness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The idler who does not exert himself when he should, who though young and strong is full of sloth, with a mind full of vain thoughts — such an indolent man does not find the path to wisdom.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that one who is able but will not exert himself misses the path.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's disgraced man who thinks he can live without effort.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a close match for the negative half of the couplet.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fallow leaf of the tree falls to the ground, when its days are gone, even so the life of men (will come to its close); Gautama, be careful all the while!”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira repeatedly urges his disciple Gautama never to be slack (apramada), because human life and its rare opportunity pass quickly.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain call to unbroken vigilance matches the Kural's scorn for anyone content to live without striving.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the Jain zeal is spiritual vigilance against karma, not the worldly ambition of the Kural, so the fit is partial.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Work is no disgrace: it is idleness which is a disgrace.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells his idle brother Perses that honour comes from labour and shame from idleness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod uses the Kural's very pairing: effort brings honour and a slack life brings disgrace.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 311 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on theoi.com; near one-to-one on disgrace, though Hesiod means farm labour rather than great deeds.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “…let this thought be present—I am rising to the work of a human being. Why then am I dissatisfied if I am going to do the things for which I exist and for which I was brought into the world?”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius rebukes his own reluctance to get out of bed, reminding himself that he exists for action.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he treats wanting to live without exertion as a betrayal of what makes a person worthy.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified on classics.mit.edu (punctuation of the dash normalised); a strong thematic fit on energy for one's proper work.

kurals.tamil:
பிறப்பொக்கும் எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் சிறப்பொவ்வா
செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமை யான்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pirappokkum ellaa uyirkkum sirappovvaa
seydhozhil vetrumai yaan.
kurals.meaning: All living beings are alike in birth; distinction differs only because of the difference in the deeds they do.
kurals.elementary: Every baby is born the same way, crying and tiny, whether in a palace or a hut. What makes people different later is what they choose to do: who helps, who works hard, who is kind. That is where real specialness comes from.
kurals.university: The couplet sets piRappu (பிறப்பு, 'birth') against siRappu (சிறப்பு, 'distinction'): the first ஒக்கும் ('is equal') for all, the second ஒவ்வா ('is not equal') because of seydhozhil vetrumai (செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமை, 'difference in the work done'). Commentators differ on the scope of uyir: Puliyur Kesikan restricts it to 'all human lives' (எல்லா மக்களுயிர்க்கும்), the older reading, while modern glosses keep 'all living beings'. They also differ on tozhil: Mu. Varadarasanar speaks of the high and low grades of occupations, whereas Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as one's deeds or skill and make the verse an explicit statement that all are equal by birth. This egalitarian reading has made the couplet one of the most frequently cited in modern Tamil debates on caste. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The humble sages, by virtue of true knowledge, see with equal vision a learned and gentle brāhmaṇa, a cow, an elephant, a dog and a dog-eater [outcaste].”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says the wise look past outward birth and see the same self in every being.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's first half: all beings are alike in birth and essence.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 5.18 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; matches equal birth, but does not address distinction through deeds, and the Gita elsewhere (4.13) ties social order to qualities and work.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Athenians that all peoples come from a single origin.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it grounds human equality in a shared birth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; covers common origin only, not the Kural's point that deeds create distinction.

islam.quote_or_event: “O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says humanity shares one origin and that nobility is measured by righteousness, not lineage.
islam.tie_back: Both halves of the Kural are here: equal origin, and distinction earned by conduct.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match on both equal birth and merit-based distinction.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And this was done due to the importance of maintaining peace among people, so that one person will not say to another: My father, i.e., progenitor, is greater than your father.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah teaches that humanity was created from a single person so that no one could claim superior ancestry.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it denies that birth can make one person higher than another.
judaism.source: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria, including Steinsaltz's interpolated gloss; strong on equal birth, silent on distinction by deeds.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by birth is one an outcast; not by birth is one a brahman. By deed one becomes an outcast, by deed one becomes a brahman.”
buddhism.explanation: Answering a brahman who insulted him, the Buddha says worth is made by action, not by birth.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural restated: birth does not differ, deeds do.
buddhism.source: Vasala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.7, v. 21 (trans. Piyadassi Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; near one-to-one match.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By one's actions one becomes a Brâhmana, or a Kshattriya, or a Vaisya, or a Sûdra.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Jayaghosha tells a sacrificing priest that a person's class is made by conduct, not by birth or ritual marks.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain canon states the Kural's point directly: distinction comes from what one does.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified); near one-to-one, from a distinct Jain canonical source.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides' Electra, Electra has been married off to a poor farmer, who treats her with honour and restraint; Orestes, seeing this, reflects that there is no sure test of a man's nobility, since a man of humble station can prove more noble than the well-born.
greek_mythology.explanation: The play uses a lowly farmer to show that nobility of character does not follow birth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it separates worth from lineage and ties it to conduct.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Electra (Orestes' speech on nobility, c. lines 367-390)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from memory of a well-known passage, not verified against a live text this session; a solid thematic match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his 44th letter Seneca tells Lucilius that philosophy does not ask about a person's pedigree, citing Plato's remark that every king comes from a race of slaves and every slave from kings, and concluding that it is the mind, not ancestry, that makes a person noble.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that long lines of ancestry mix high and low, so only character can confer nobility.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca, like Valluvar, says birth is common to all and distinction is earned.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 44 (trans. R. M. Gummere)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the live text could not be loaded this session, so no wording is quoted.

kurals.tamil:
மேலிருந்தும் மேலல்லார் மேலல்லர் கீழிருந்தும்
கீழல்லார் கீழல் லவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Melirundhum melallaar melallar keezhirundhum
keezhallaar keezhal lavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who are not truly high are not high even when they sit high; those who are not base are not low even when they are placed low.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a bully sitting on the tallest chair in class, and a kind child sitting on the floor. The tall chair does not make the bully great, and the floor does not make the kind child small. Who you are matters more than where you sit.
kurals.university: The verse is a chiasmus built on mel (மேல், 'above, superior') and keezh (கீழ், 'below, base'), each used both for physical or social position and for moral quality: melirundhum melallaar melallar, 'though they be above, those not superior are not superior'. Puliyur Kesikan makes the image literal, 'though they sit on high seats' (உயர்ந்த ஆசனங்களிலே), and ties superiority to having done 'deeds hard to do', linking back to Kural 971; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar render mel as high office or position. Pope's 'men of lofty line' reads it as birth, which carries the theme on from Kural 972. The repeated negatives (அல்லார், அல்லர், அல்லவர்) give the couplet its characteristic Valluvan density. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Yaksha's questioning of Yudhishthira, the Yaksha asks what makes a Brahmana, and Yudhishthira answers that it is neither birth nor study nor learning but conduct alone, which must always be guarded.
hinduism.explanation: Yudhishthira insists that rank is earned by behaviour, not inherited by birth or bought by learning.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it denies that a high station makes one high without the matching character.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana (Aranyaka) Parva, Yaksha Prashna episode (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the Ganguli text was not loaded this session, so no wording or section number is quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.”
christianity.explanation: Mary's song proclaims that God overturns the order of high and low.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says that sitting in a high seat does not secure true height.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the 'seats' image matches closely, though Luke speaks of divine reversal rather than inner quality.

islam.quote_or_event: “Verily Allah does not look to your faces and your wealth but He looks to your heart and to your deeds.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that God's measure of a person ignores appearance and riches and looks to heart and action.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's true height and lowness are measured the same way, by inner quality rather than outward place.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; strong thematic match, though it does not use the high/low imagery.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I saw an inverted world. Those above, i.e., those who are considered important in this world, were below, insignificant, while those below, i.e., those who are insignificant in this world, were above. He said to him: My son, you have seen a clear world.”
judaism.explanation: Rav Yosef, returning from near death, reports that the true world reverses this world's rankings, and his father calls that the clear view.
judaism.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's claim that worldly position and true standing do not match.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 50a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria including Steinsaltz's glosses; a near match on high and low positions versus true worth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A monk is not an elder because his head is gray. He is but ripe in age, and he is called one grown old in vain.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the title of elder means nothing without the virtues that should go with it.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it denies that outward rank alone makes one truly senior.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; matches the first half of the couplet only.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The value of penance has become visible, birth appears of no value! Look at the holy Harikêsa, the son of a Svapâka, whose power is so great.”
jainism.explanation: Priests who mocked the low-born monk Harikesa are humbled, and the onlookers proclaim that his austerities, not his birth, decide his worth.
jainism.tie_back: Harikesa is the Kural's person placed low by birth who is in no way low.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified); the same lecture shows the haughty priests as the high who are not high.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Odysseus returns home disguised as a ragged beggar and is mocked in his own hall by the suitors, who occupy the seats of honour while behaving shamefully, until he reveals himself as the true king.
greek_mythology.explanation: The epic contrasts the low appearance of a noble man with the lofty places held by base men.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The suitors are high without being high, and the beggar-king is low without being low.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased narrative; a reasonable illustration, though the disguise is a ruse rather than a real low station.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “These reasonings are unconnected: ‘I am richer than you, therefore I am better’; ‘I am more eloquent than you, therefore I am better.’ … But you, after all, are neither property nor style.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus says that having more of something outward never makes a person better.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it refuses to let external standing define who is truly superior.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu (middle sentence elided); strong on the first half of the couplet.

kurals.tamil:
ஒருமை மகளிரே போலப் பெருமையும்
தன்னைத்தான் கொண்டொழுகின் உண்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Orumai magalire polap perumaiyum
thannaiththaan kondozhugin undu.
kurals.meaning: Like a woman of single-hearted faithfulness, greatness too exists only for the one who guards himself.
kurals.elementary: A promise only stays a promise if you keep it, even when nobody is watching. Valluvar says greatness is the same: it is not a prize someone hands you, it stays with you only while you keep guarding your own good behaviour.
kurals.university: The simile turns on orumai magalir (ஒருமை மகளிர், 'women of oneness'), which the commentators uniformly read as women of undivided chastity (கற்பு, karpu): Mu. Varadarasanar says ஒரு தன்மையான கற்புடைய மகளிர், and Puliyur Kesikan describes women whose minds do not waver and who guard themselves without lapsing. The point of comparison is thannaiththaan kondozhugin (தன்னைத்தான் கொண்டொழுகின், 'if one conducts oneself holding oneself'), that is, self-guarding: greatness, like chastity, cannot be imposed from outside and is lost by a single lapse. The gendered simile reflects the period; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it more inwardly as being true to oneself. Pope's 'Like single-hearted women, greatness too, / Exists while to itself is true' keeps the ambiguity. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One must deliver himself with the help of his mind, and not degrade himself. The mind is the friend of the conditioned soul, and his enemy as well.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that each person must raise himself and guard against bringing himself down.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes a person's elevation depend on his own self-guarding.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.5 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; matches self-guarding but not the chastity simile.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs urges constant guarding of one's inner self as the source of everything one becomes.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise says greatness lasts only while one keeps guard over oneself.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; good on self-guarding, without the faithfulness simile.

islam.quote_or_event: “He has succeeded who purifies it, And he has failed who instills it [with corruption].”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an ties success or failure to how a person tends their own soul.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes standing depend on keeping oneself pure and guarded.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; parallel on self-tending, not on the chastity image.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: ‘He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city’ (Proverbs 16:32).”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines might as mastery over one's own impulses.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it locates true greatness in holding oneself in check.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; strong on self-mastery as greatness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One truly is the protector of oneself; who else could the protector be? With oneself fully controlled, one gains a mastery that is hard to gain.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says no one else can guard a person; self-control yields a rare mastery.
buddhism.tie_back: Close to the Kural: greatness exists only for the one who guards himself.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a close match on self-guarding, minus the simile.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Rathanemi lecture, the nun Rajimati, sheltering in a cave after being caught in rain, is approached by the monk Rathanemi, who loses his composure; she stays firm, rebukes him for wavering in his vows, and her steadfastness brings him back to the discipline.
jainism.explanation: Rajimati, revered in Jain tradition for her constancy, guards herself and even restores another's resolve.
jainism.tie_back: She embodies both halves of the Kural's simile: single-hearted faithfulness and the greatness that comes from guarding oneself.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22 (Rathanemi) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Story summarised, not quoted; the lecture was not reloaded this session, so details are given only in outline.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the underworld scene of the Odyssey, the shade of Agamemnon praises Penelope for keeping faith with Odysseus through twenty years of pressure from the suitors, and declares that the fame of her virtue will never die.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope's renown rests entirely on her steady self-keeping.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She is the Greek counterpart of the Kural's single-hearted woman whose honour lasts because she guards herself.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a close match for the simile itself rather than for the general point.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Republic IV Socrates explains temperance as an ordering and mastery of pleasures and desires, the condition people point to when they call someone 'master of himself'.
philosophy.explanation: Plato treats self-mastery as the inner order on which every other virtue depends.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes excellence a matter of keeping hold of oneself.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not quoted; a reasonable but general match.

kurals.tamil:
பெருமை யுடையவர் ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றின்
அருமை உடைய செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Perumai yudaiyavar aatruvaar aatrin
arumai udaiya seyal.
kurals.meaning: Those who have greatness will accomplish, in the proper way, deeds that are hard for others to do.
kurals.elementary: Some jobs are so hard that most people give up, like building a tall tower of blocks without it falling. A great person keeps going and does it carefully, the right way, until it stands.
kurals.university: The verse plays on aatru (ஆற்று), used twice: aatruvaar ('they will accomplish') and aatrin, which commentators take either as 'by the (proper) way' (ஆறு, 'path, method') or as 'if they set about it'. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the first: 'in the way proper to it' (உரிய நெறியில்). Puliyur Kesikan adds 'even when they have fallen into poverty' (வறுமையான போதும்), the traditional gloss also reflected in Pope's explanation '(Though reduced) the great will be able to perform…', which holds that greatness shows itself in rare deeds even without resources. The couplet makes concrete the 'deeds hard for others' that Kural 971 called the light of a person. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A man engaged in devotional service rids himself of both good and bad reactions even in this life. Therefore strive for yoga, which is the art of all work.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita's famous phrase yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam calls disciplined action a skill or art in doing work.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's great person does hard things the right way, which is skill in action.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.50 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; the 'art of work' idea fits, but Prabhupada's rendering is devotional and the verse is not about rare deeds.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that, strengthened by Christ, he can face anything, whether plenty or want.
christianity.tie_back: It echoes the Kural's confidence that the great can carry out what others cannot, even in hardship.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; next-best match, since the strength is God-given and the context is contentment rather than achieving rare deeds.

islam.quote_or_event: In Surat al-Kahf, Dhul-Qarnayn is asked by a threatened people to build a barrier against Gog and Magog; he organises the work, has iron blocks filled in and molten copper poured over them, completes the barrier, and attributes it to his Lord's mercy.
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents a great ruler who accomplishes an enormous task by careful, proper method.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's great person, he does what others could not, and does it the right way.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased narrative; a reasonable but partial match.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In a place where there are no men, strive to be a man.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel teaches that when no one else steps up, one must take on the task oneself.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's great person, who undertakes what others leave undone.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:5 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; strong on taking up what others avoid, silent on doing it properly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easy to do are things that are bad and harmful to oneself. But exceedingly difficult to do are things that are good and beneficial.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada notes that the good path is the hard one.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's great people are those who take up exactly these hard, worthwhile deeds.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it names the rarity of good deeds but not who achieves them.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Acaranga Sutra and Kalpa Sutra describe Mahavira's more than twelve years of austerities after renouncing the world, enduring hardship and hostility with equanimity, until he attained omniscience (kevala jnana).
jainism.explanation: Jain scripture presents Mahavira's long, disciplined ascetic effort as the supreme example of a hard task carried through by the proper path.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows greatness as completing what others cannot, in the right manner.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.8 and Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the Jain 'rare deed' is renunciation and self-conquest, not worldly accomplishment, so the fit is partial.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Set the labour of cleaning King Augeas' vast and long-neglected cattle yard in a single day, Heracles breached the yard's foundations and diverted the rivers Alpheus and Peneus to wash it out.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles achieves an apparently impossible task by finding the right method rather than by brute effort alone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's rare deed done in the proper way.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a good match on rare deed and right method.

philosophy.quote_or_event: At the close of the Ethics Spinoza admits that the way to blessedness he has described is very hard and is rarely found, remarking that all excellent things are as difficult as they are rare.
philosophy.explanation: Spinoza links excellence with difficulty and rarity.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural makes the same link: the great are known by deeds that are rare because they are hard.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics V, Prop. 42, Scholium (trans. R. H. M. Elwes)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased rather than quoted, since the text was not verified live this session; a strong thematic fit.

kurals.tamil:
சிறியார் உணர்ச்சியுள் இல்லை பெரியாரைப்
பேணிக்கொள் வேமென்னும் நோக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Siriyaar unarchchiyul illai periyaaraip
penikkol vemennum nokku.
kurals.meaning: The aim 'Let us cherish the great and make their way our own' does not arise in the minds of small-minded people.
kurals.elementary: When a great teacher comes to school, some children run to listen and learn, hoping to become like her. Others just shrug and keep playing. Valluvar says wanting to learn from great people is itself a sign of a big heart.
kurals.university: Siriyaar (சிறியார், 'the small') is the counter-term to periyaar (பெரியார், 'the great') throughout this chapter and the next. The key phrase is peNikkoLvem (பேணிக்கொள்வேம், 'we will cherish and take to ourselves'): Puliyur Kesikan reads it as 'we will serve the great and attain their nature ourselves' (அவரியல்பை நாமும் அடைவோம்), Solomon Pappaiah as following them and preserving their tradition, and Mu. Varadarasanar as honouring them, which the small cannot do because they do not perceive the greatness at all. Nokku (நோக்கு, 'aim, outlook') and unarchchi (உணர்ச்சி, 'feeling, awareness') make the point psychological: the lack is in perception, not merely in will. Pope renders 'As votaries of the truly great we will ourselves enroll'. The text matches on both sites, with ytamizh omitting the final full stop.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Just try to learn the truth by approaching a spiritual master. Inquire from him submissively and render service unto him. The self-realized souls can impart knowledge unto you because they have seen the truth.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna urges Arjuna to approach the wise, serve them and learn from them.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the 'aim to cherish the great' that the Kural says small minds lack.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 4.34 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; it describes the positive attitude the Kural presupposes.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs says that seeking the company of the wise makes one wise.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's great-hearted seek the great; the small do not, and stay small.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; matches the value of keeping company with the great.

islam.quote_or_event: “Moses said to him, ‘May I follow you on [the condition] that you teach me from what you have been taught of sound judgement?’”
islam.explanation: Even the prophet Moses humbly asks to follow and learn from a wiser servant of God.
islam.tie_back: He shows the outlook the Kural finds lacking in small minds: the wish to follow the great and absorb their wisdom.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a positive mirror of the Kural's negative statement.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let thy house be a house of meeting for the Sages and sit in the very dust of their feet, and drink in their words with thirst.”
judaism.explanation: Yose ben Yoezer urges eager, humble attachment to the wise.
judaism.tie_back: This thirst to cherish the great is exactly what the Kural says the small never feel.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:4 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a strong positive counterpart.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though all his life a fool associates with a wise man, he no more comprehends the Truth than a spoon tastes the flavor of the soup.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says a fool can sit beside the wise for a lifetime and absorb nothing.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's point exactly: the small have no inner capacity to take on the nature of the great.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match.

jainism.quote_or_event: The first lecture of the Uttaradhyayana, 'On Discipline' (vinaya), contrasts the well-behaved disciple, who stays near his teacher, carries out his instructions and understands his wishes, with the ill-behaved disciple who neglects the teacher and so gains nothing.
jainism.explanation: Jain monastic teaching treats reverent attachment to the teacher as the gateway to knowledge.
jainism.tie_back: The ill-behaved disciple is the Kural's small person who has no wish to cherish the great.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 1, 'On Discipline' (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Summarised from the lecture's overall argument, not quoted; the lecture was not reloaded this session.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Urged by Athena, the young Telemachus sails to Pylos and Sparta to seek out the aged Nestor and King Menelaus, learning from them about his father and about how great men act.
greek_mythology.explanation: Telemachus' coming of age begins with going out to learn from the great.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He shows the outlook the Kural says the small lack: wanting to learn from great men and become like them.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a positive mirror image and a looser fit than the Buddhist parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato's allegory of the cave, the prisoners who have only ever seen shadows mock the one who returns from the light and would even kill anyone who tried to lead them upward.
philosophy.explanation: Plato portrays people who cannot recognise or welcome a mind greater than their own.
philosophy.tie_back: The prisoners are the Kural's small people, for whom honouring the great is simply not part of their outlook.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a strong illustration of the small failing to perceive the great.

kurals.tamil:
இறப்பே புரிந்த தொழிற்றாம் சிறப்புந்தான்
சீரல் லவர்கண் படின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Irappe purindha thozhitraam sirappundhaan
seeral lavarkan padin.
kurals.meaning: Even distinction, when it falls to unworthy people, turns into deeds that overstep every limit.
kurals.elementary: Give a bossy child the job of class leader and he might start ordering everyone around and showing off. The badge was meant for helping, but in the wrong hands it turns into bullying.
kurals.university: Sirappu (சிறப்பு, 'eminence, distinction') here covers whatever raises a person; Solomon Pappaiah lists money, learning and office, and Pope's explanation 'nobility of birth, wealth and learning' reflects the traditional commentarial list. When it reaches seeral lavar (சீரல்லவர், 'those without worth'), it becomes irappe purindha thozhitru (இறப்பே புரிந்த தொழிற்று), 'of the nature of acting only in excess': irappu (இறப்பு) is taken by Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar as 'overstepping the bounds' (வரம்பு மீறிய செயல்) and by Kesikan as being driven into arrogance. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads irappu as 'destruction', a minority gloss. The couplet is the negative counterpart to Kural 975: the same eminence that lets the great do rare deeds makes the small insolent. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Self-complacent and always impudent, deluded by wealth and false prestige, they sometimes proudly perform sacrifices in name only, without following any rules or regulations.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the demoniac as people whom wealth and prestige make impudent and lawless.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows advantages turning into insolence and disregard of every limit in unworthy hands.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.17 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a close match on distinction producing overreach.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For three things the earth is disquieted, and for four which it cannot bear: For a servant when he reigneth; and a fool when he is filled with meat;”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs names the unfit person suddenly raised to power as something the world cannot bear.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's distinction falling to the unworthy and turning into excess.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a close match, though the proverb's 'servant' framing reflects its own social assumptions.

islam.quote_or_event: “No! [But] indeed, man transgresses Because he sees himself self-sufficient.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says a person oversteps bounds once he feels he needs no one.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's 'deeds that overstep the limit' arise in the same way when the unworthy gain distinction.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong on advantage breeding transgression.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When you have eaten your fill, and have built fine houses to live in, and your herds and flocks have multiplied, and your silver and gold have increased, and everything you own has prospered, beware lest your heart grow haughty and you forget the Eternal your God…”
judaism.explanation: Moses warns Israel that prosperity can make the heart haughty.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it warns that advantages can turn into arrogance.
judaism.source: Deuteronomy 8:12-14 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (small capitals normalised); a warning to all, rather than specifically about the unworthy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To his own ruin the fool gains knowledge, for it cleaves his head and destroys his innate goodness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that in a fool even knowledge becomes destructive.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's point: a distinction such as learning, held by the unworthy, turns to harm.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a close match for one of the distinctions the commentators list.

jainism.quote_or_event: Samantabhadra's householder manual lists eight kinds of pride (mada) to be given up: pride in knowledge, honour, family, caste, power, attainments, austerity and bodily beauty, warning that one who looks down on others through such pride offends against the faith itself.
jainism.explanation: Jain ethics treats every advantage of birth, learning, power or beauty as a possible source of corrupting pride.
jainism.tie_back: The eight madas are exactly the Kural's distinctions that, in the unworthy, breed overbearing conduct.
jainism.source: Ratnakaranda Shravakachara of Samantabhadra, vv. 25-26 (tr. Champat Rai Jain)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not quoted; the verse numbers follow the standard numbering but were not re-checked live this session.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ixion, after being purified by Zeus and honoured with a place among the gods on Olympus, repaid the favour by trying to seduce Hera, and was bound for ever to a fiery wheel.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pindar tells the story as a warning about a man who could not bear his good fortune.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ixion is the Kural's unworthy man whose distinction turns at once into outrageous excess.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased myth; a strong match on undeserved honour producing hubris.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Rhetoric Aristotle sketches the characters that wealth and power produce, observing that the newly rich in particular become insolent and arrogant, behaving as though they possessed every good.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle analyses how fortune tends to warp the character of those who receive it.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he notes that distinction in unfit hands turns into insolence.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric II.16 (trans. W. Rhys Roberts)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not quoted; the chapter was not reloaded this session.

kurals.tamil:
பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை சிறுமை
அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Paniyumaam endrum perumai sirumai
aniyumaam thannai viyandhu.
kurals.meaning: Greatness always bows in humility; littleness decks itself out, marvelling at itself.
kurals.elementary: A tree heavy with fruit bends its branches low, while an empty stalk sticks straight up. Valluvar says truly great people are like the fruit tree: they stay humble, while small people keep showing off.
kurals.university: The couplet sets two verbs in parallel, paniyum (பணியும், 'bends, submits') and aniyum (அணியும், 'adorns'), with the expletive -aam (ஆம்) giving the tone of a settled maxim and endrum (என்றும், 'always') applying to both. Thannai viyandhu (தன்னை வியந்து, 'admiring itself') explains the adorning: littleness dresses itself up in its own praise. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'greatness walks in humility at all times, littleness praises itself', and Kalaignar adds that the small lie puffed up (இறுமாந்து). Pope's 'Greatness humbly bends, but littleness always / Spreads out its plumes' turns aniyum into a peacock image not in the Tamil. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Humility; pridelessness; nonviolence; tolerance; simplicity; approaching a bona fide spiritual master; cleanliness; steadiness; self-control…”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna's list of the marks of true knowledge begins with humility and pridelessness (amānitvam, adambhitvam).
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it puts humility first among the marks of the truly great.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 13.8-12 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (opening excerpt) on vedabase.io; matches the humility half only.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that self-exaltation leads down and humility leads up.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts set the humble bow of greatness against the self-promotion of littleness.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a close match on both halves.

islam.quote_or_event: “Charity does not decrease wealth, no one forgives another except that Allah increases his honor, and no one humbles himself for the sake of Allah except that Allah raises his status.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that humility raises a person's standing.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes humble bowing the true sign and source of greatness.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; strong on humility, without the self-praise contrast.

judaism.quote_or_event: “…anyone who humbles himself, the Holy One, Blessed be He, exalts him, and anyone who exalts himself, the Holy One, Blessed be He, humbles him. Anyone who seeks greatness, greatness flees from him, and, conversely, anyone who flees from greatness, greatness seeks him.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud explains that Beit Hillel's rulings prevailed because they were humble, and draws a general lesson about greatness.
judaism.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's pairing of humble greatness with self-exalting smallness.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 13b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a near one-to-one match on humility and greatness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘Let both laymen and monks think that it was done by me. In every work, great and small, let them follow me’ — such is the ambition of the fool; thus his desire and pride increase.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada portrays the fool who wants credit for everything.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's littleness, decking itself out in self-admiration.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; matches the second half of the couplet closely.

jainism.quote_or_event: After defeating his elder brother Bharata, Bahubali renounced the world and stood in motionless meditation for a year, but omniscience would not come because pride kept him from going to bow to his younger brothers, who had become monks before him; when his sisters made him see this and he resolved to go and bow, he attained kevala jnana.
jainism.explanation: In Jain tradition even the greatest austerity is blocked by pride and completed by humility.
jainism.tie_back: Bahubali's greatness is fulfilled only when it bows, just as the Kural says.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacaritra I (Life of Rishabha) (tr. Helen M. Johnson)
jainism._accuracy_note: Well-attested Svetambara narrative, summarised rather than quoted; a near-direct illustration of the couplet.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Niobe boasted that with her many children she was more worthy of worship than the goddess Leto, who had only two; Apollo and Artemis killed her children, and the grieving Niobe was turned to weeping stone.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes self-glorifying boast the classic Greek form of fatal pride.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Niobe is the Kural's littleness that adorns itself with its own praise.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased myth; a strong match for the self-praising half of the couplet.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Apology Socrates explains the oracle's verdict by saying that the reputedly wise man he questioned knew nothing yet thought he knew, while he himself neither knew nor thought he knew, and so was wiser only in that small way.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates' wisdom consists in an honest humility that refuses to claim more than it has.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates is the Kural's greatness that bows, and his self-satisfied interlocutors are the littleness that admires itself.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a well-known passage, not re-verified live this session.

kurals.tamil:
பெருமை பெருமிதம் இன்மை சிறுமை
பெருமிதம் ஊர்ந்து விடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Perumai perumidham inmai sirumai
perumidham oorndhu vidal.
kurals.meaning: Greatness is the absence of arrogance; littleness is to ride on arrogance all the way.
kurals.elementary: A real champion says, 'Thanks, my team helped me.' Someone who isn't much of a champion struts around shouting, 'I'm the best!' Valluvar says being great means not puffing yourself up at all.
kurals.university: The couplet defines both terms through a single word, perumidham (பெருமிதம், 'swagger, pride'), which etymologically contains the same peru- ('great') as perumai: greatness is its absence (inmai, இன்மை), littleness is perumidham oorndhu vidal (பெருமிதம் ஊர்ந்து விடல்), 'mounting and riding on pride'. Mu. Varadarasanar reads oorndhu vidal as 'pride growing until it reaches its limit and stopping there', while Solomon Pappaiah sharpens the contrast: having cause for pride yet not being proud is greatness, being proud without cause is littleness. Pope's 'Riding on car of vanity supreme' keeps the image of mounting a vehicle. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Pride, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance – these qualities belong to those of demoniac nature, O son of Pṛthā.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names pride, arrogance and conceit as the first marks of the demoniac nature.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it defines the lower nature by the presence of conceit.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.4 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a close match on littleness as conceit.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Philippians to act without vainglory and in humility.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's definition of greatness: the absence of conceit.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong match on the first half.

islam.quote_or_event: “He who has in his heart the weight of a mustard seed of pride shall not enter Paradise. … Pride is disdaining the truth (out of self-conceit) and contempt for the people.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet condemns even a trace of pride and defines it as self-conceit and contempt for others.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats conceit as the defining mark of the lowly soul.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com (middle exchange elided); a strong match.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Now Moses himself was very humble, more so than any other human being on earth.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah singles out the greatest prophet for his humility.
judaism.tie_back: Moses is the Kural's greatness defined by the absence of pride.
judaism.source: Numbers 12:3 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; illustrates the first half by example rather than definition.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least to that extent, but a fool who thinks himself wise is a fool indeed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that conceit about one's own wisdom is the surest sign of folly.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes inflated self-regard the mark of littleness.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a related but narrower point about intellectual conceit.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Dasavaikalika Sutra teaches that pride (mana) destroys humility (vinaya), and that pride is to be conquered by softness or humility (mardava), just as anger is conquered by calm, deceit by straightforwardness and greed by contentment.
jainism.explanation: In Jain doctrine pride is one of the four passions (kashayas) that bind karma, and its remedy is humility.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain ideal of conquering pride by humility is the Kural's definition of greatness as freedom from conceit.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; verse numbers differ across editions and the wording was not checked live this session.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phaethon, eager to prove his divine parentage, insisted on driving the chariot of his father the Sun; unable to control the horses, he scorched the earth until Zeus struck him down with a thunderbolt.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows vanity literally mounting a chariot it cannot manage.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Phaethon is a vivid picture of the Kural's littleness 'riding on pride' to ruin.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the riding image matches Pope's rendering, though the myth stresses rashness as much as conceit.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In discussing greatness of soul, Aristotle describes the vain man as one who thinks himself worthy of great things when he is not, and who parades his supposed merits in dress and display and is shown up by events.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle separates real greatness of soul from the vanity that claims it falsely.
philosophy.tie_back: His vain man is the Kural's littleness riding on pride without any ground for it.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; Aristotle's great-souled man claims honour he deserves, so he is less humble than the Kural's ideal.

kurals.tamil:
அற்றம் மறைக்கும் பெருமை சிறுமைதான்
குற்றமே கூறி விடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Atram maraikkum perumai sirumaidhaan
kutrame koori vidum.
kurals.meaning: Greatness covers up the weaknesses of others; littleness speaks of nothing but their faults.
kurals.elementary: If a friend trips and falls in the playground, a kind person helps them up and doesn't laugh. A mean person runs around telling everyone, 'Did you see him fall?' Valluvar says greatness is the helping hand, and smallness is the tattletale.
kurals.university: Atram (அற்றம்) means a weak, exposed or shameful point, literally a gap or defenceless state; maraikkum (மறைக்கும்) is 'conceals'. Against this, sirumai kutrame kooRi vidum (குற்றமே கூறி விடும்): 'littleness will speak out only faults', the emphatic -e (ஏ) on kutram marking that it says nothing else. Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah expand the contrast: the great speak of others' merits and hide their failings, the small hide their merits and broadcast their failings. Pope's 'Greatness will hide a neighbour's shame; / Meanness his faults to all the world proclaim' follows this reading. The chapter thus ends on how the great treat others, after nine couplets on how they hold themselves. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…truthfulness; freedom from anger; renunciation; tranquillity; aversion to faultfinding; compassion for all living entities…”
hinduism.explanation: Among the divine qualities Krishna lists apaiśunam, aversion to faultfinding.
hinduism.tie_back: It names as a godly trait the very restraint the Kural calls greatness.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.1-3 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (excerpt) on vedabase.io; matches the refusal to find fault, not the active covering of others' weakness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins.”
christianity.explanation: Peter teaches that love covers over others' failings.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes covering others' faults the sign of a large heart.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a close match on the first half.

islam.quote_or_event: “…he who conceals (the faults) of a Muslim, Allah would conceal his faults in the world and in the Hereafter.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet promises that whoever covers a fellow believer's faults will have his own covered by God.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's greatness that hides another's weakness.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com (excerpt from a longer hadith); a near-direct match on concealing faults.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father’s nakedness and told his two brothers outside. But Shem and Japheth took a cloth, placed it against both their backs and, walking backward, they covered their father’s nakedness…”
judaism.explanation: When Noah lies exposed, Ham broadcasts it while Shem and Japheth cover him without looking.
judaism.tie_back: The story enacts the Kural almost literally: greatness covers the exposed weakness, littleness tells it.
judaism.source: Genesis 9:22-23 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a near one-to-one illustration of both halves.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let none find fault with others; let none see the omissions and commissions of others. But let one see one's own acts, done and undone.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells his followers to watch their own conduct rather than catalogue others' failings.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it rejects the small habit of dwelling on others' faults.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; matches the second half most closely.

jainism.quote_or_event: Among the eight limbs of right faith (samyag-darshana), Jain teaching lists upaguhana: covering up the faults that weak or ignorant followers bring upon the path, rather than exposing them to public reproach.
jainism.explanation: Concealing a fellow believer's lapse is treated as a component of right faith itself.
jainism.tie_back: Upaguhana is very close to the Kural's greatness that hides others' weakness.
jainism.source: Ratnakaranda Shravakachara of Samantabhadra, v. 15 (tr. Champat Rai Jain)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the Jain limb is aimed at protecting the reputation of the path and its fellow believers, a slightly narrower scope than the Kural.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the assembly before Troy, Thersites, described as the ugliest and most foul-mouthed man in the army, rails at Agamemnon and the leaders, listing their failings to the troops, until Odysseus silences him with his staff.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer portrays Thersites as the mean man whose speech consists of finding fault.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Thersites is the Kural's littleness that does nothing but proclaim others' faults.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; matches only the second half, and Thersites' complaints are not wholly unjust.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The marks of a proficient are, that he censures no one, praises no one, blames no one, accuses no one, says nothing concerning himself as being anybody, or knowing anything…”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus lists refusing to censure, blame or accuse others among the signs of moral progress.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it counts restraint from exposing others' faults as a mark of the great.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; strong on not finding fault, though it does not speak of covering others' weaknesses.
